content.prompt: In the diagram to the right, $PQRS$ is a parallelogram. Prove that $\angle S=\angle Q$ and $\angle P=\angle R$, as presented earlier.

spec.description: Unshaded parallelogram PQRS. P and Q are the upper vertices; S and R are the lower vertices. Horizontal sides carry matching double parallel arrows, and sloping sides carry matching single parallel arrows. Ordinary source blue strokes are rendered black in house style.
spec.mathematics: PQ is parallel to SR; PS is parallel to QR. No angle values, diagonal or supplementary constructions are supplied.
spec.answerVisibility: Only the given parallelogram, vertex labels and parallel marks are visible.

answer.short:
$\angle S=\angle Q$ and $\angle P=\angle R$.

Each pair is supplementary to the same adjacent angle, using the parallel sides.
answer.worked:
Since $PQ\parallel SR$, co-interior angles on transversal $PS$ give
$$\angle S=180^{\circ}-\angle P.$$
Since $PS\parallel QR$, co-interior angles on transversal $PQ$ give
$$\angle Q=180^{\circ}-\angle P.$$
Therefore $\angle S=\angle Q$.

Also, since $PQ\parallel SR$, co-interior angles on transversal $QR$ give
$$\begin{align*}\angle R&=180^{\circ}-\angle Q\\\angle R&=180^{\circ}-(180^{\circ}-\angle P)\\\angle R&=\angle P.\end{align*}$$
Hence $\angle P=\angle R$.

content.prompt: In the diagram to the right, $XYZW$ is a parallelogram. $M$ is the point of intersection of $XZ$ and $YW$. Prove that $XM=ZM$, as presented earlier.

spec.description: Unshaded parallelogram with single parallel arrows on XY and WZ, double parallel arrows on YZ and XW, and red dashed diagonals meeting at a red point M. Ordinary source-blue outlines and arrows become house black.

spec.answerVisibility: Only the supplied geometry, parallel marks, diagonals and point labels are visible.

answer.short:
$XM=ZM$.

$\triangle XYM\equiv\triangle ZWM$ by AAS, so their matching sides $XM$ and $ZM$ are equal.
answer.worked:
In triangles $XYM$ and $ZWM$:

$\angle YXM=\angle WZM$ (alternate angles, $XY\parallel WZ$).

$\angle XYM=\angle ZWM$ (alternate angles, $XY\parallel WZ$).

$XY=ZW$ (opposite sides of parallelogram $XYZW$).

Therefore $\triangle XYM\equiv\triangle ZWM$ (AAS).

Hence $XM=ZM$ (matching sides of congruent triangles).

A rhombus is a parallelogram. In triangles $PQM$ and $RSM$:
$$\begin{align*}\angle QPM&=\angle SRM &&\text{(alternate angles, }PQ\parallel SR\text{)}\\\angle PQM&=\angle RSM &&\text{(alternate angles, }PQ\parallel SR\text{)}\\PQ&=RS &&\text{(sides of a rhombus).}\end{align*}$$
Thus $\triangle PQM\equiv\triangle RSM$ (AAS). Hence $QM=MS$ and $PM=MR$ (matching sides of congruent triangles).

For perpendicularity, $PQ=PS$, $QR=SR$ and $PR$ is common. Therefore $\triangle PQR\equiv\triangle PSR$ (SSS), so $\angle QRP=\angle PRS$.

Let $\angle RQS=\alpha$ and $\angle QRP=\beta$. Since $QR=RS$, the base angles of isosceles triangle $QRS$ give $\angle QSR=\alpha$. Also $\angle QRS=2\beta$. Therefore
$$\begin{align*}2\alpha+2\beta&=180^\circ &&\text{(angle sum of }\triangle QRS\text{)}\\\alpha+\beta&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
In triangle $QMR$,
$$\begin{align*}\angle QMR&=180^\circ-(\alpha+\beta)\\\angle QMR&=180^\circ-90^\circ\\\angle QMR&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Thus the diagonals bisect each other at right angles.

The constructed quadrilateral is a parallelogram. Both pairs of parallel sides have the same perpendicular separation, so adjacent sides are equal; hence all four sides are equal.

answer.worked:
Both pairs of opposite sides are parallel by construction, so $ABCD$ is a parallelogram. Let the ruler width be $w$. The perpendicular separation of each pair of opposite sides is $w$.

First suppose the parallelogram has an acute angle. Choose an acute vertex and, for this proof, call it $A$, with adjacent vertices $B$ and $D$. Drop perpendiculars from $B$ to the line $AD$ at $E$, and from $D$ to the line $AB$ at $F$.

$$\begin{align*}\angle AEB&=\angle AFD=90^\circ,\\\angle EAB&=\angle FAD,\\BE&=DF=w.\end{align*}$$
Therefore, $\triangle AEB\equiv\triangle AFD$ by AAS, and $AB=AD$ by matching sides.

Opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal, so $AB=CD$ and $AD=BC$. Hence $AB=BC=CD=DA$, and the construction produces a rhombus.

content.prompt: A quadrilateral has all four sides equal and two equal diagonals. Prove it is a square.

answer.short: The four triangles formed by taking three consecutive vertices are congruent by SSS. Their corresponding angles show that all four interior angles of the quadrilateral are equal, so each is $90^\circ$. With four equal sides, the quadrilateral is a square.
answer.worked:
Label the vertices $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ in order. The givens are $AB=BC=CD=DA$ and $AC=BD$.

Each of $\triangle ABC$, $\triangle BCD$, $\triangle CDA$ and $\triangle DAB$ has two sides equal to a side of the quadrilateral and its third side equal to a diagonal. Hence,
$$\triangle ABC\equiv\triangle BCD\equiv\triangle CDA\equiv\triangle DAB\quad\text{(SSS).}$$
Matching angles of these congruent triangles give
$$\angle ABC=\angle BCD=\angle CDA=\angle DAB.$$
Let each interior angle be $\theta$. By the angle sum of a quadrilateral,
$$\begin{align*}4\theta&=360^\circ\\\theta&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Thus all four angles are right angles, so $ABCD$ is a rectangle. All four sides are also equal; therefore $ABCD$ is a square.

answer.worked:
Let $\angle DAQ=\alpha$. Since $ABCD$ is a square, $DA=CD$ and $\angle ADQ=\angle DCR=90^\circ$.

In $\triangle DAQ$,
$$\angle AQD=90^\circ-\alpha.$$
Since $AQ\perp DR$ and $DQ$ lies on $DC$,
$$\angle CDR=90^\circ-\angle AQD=\alpha.$$
Thus $\angle DAQ=\angle CDR$, $\angle ADQ=\angle DCR$, and $DA=CD$.

Therefore $\triangle DAQ\equiv\triangle CDR$ (AAS), so $AQ=DR$ (matching sides of congruent triangles).

children.label: b
children.prompt: Suppose that two lines $m$ and $n$ are perpendicular and that each line intersects opposite edges of the square $ABCD$. Show that the intervals cut out by the square on $m$ and $n$ are equal in length.

answer.short:
The two intervals have equal length.

Translate them to intervals $AQ$ and $DR$ as in part a; translation preserves length and perpendicularity.
answer.worked:
Choose the orientation of the square and interchange $m$ and $n$ if necessary so that the interval on $m$ joins $AB$ to $DC$, sloping towards $C$, and the interval on $n$ joins $AD$ to $BC$, sloping towards $B$.

Translate the first interval parallel to $AB$ until its endpoint on $AB$ is $A$. Its other endpoint is a point $Q$ on $DC$: the horizontal displacement is unchanged and is no greater than a side of the square.

Translate the second interval parallel to $AD$ until its endpoint on $AD$ is $D$. Its other endpoint is a point $R$ on $BC$: the vertical displacement is unchanged and is no greater than a side of the square.

Translations preserve lengths and directions, so $AQ\perp DR$. Part a gives $AQ=DR$. Each translated interval has its original length, hence the intervals cut out on $m$ and $n$ are equal in length.

Thus $AC$ bisects the angle at $A$. Since $AB=BC$, triangle $ABC$ is isosceles, so $\angle BCA=\angle BAC=\alpha=\angle DCA$. Thus $AC$ also bisects the angle at $C$.

Join $BD$. Let $\angle ABD=\beta$. Since $AB\parallel DC$, $\angle BDC=\beta$ (alternate angles). Since $BC=CD$, triangle $BCD$ is isosceles, so $\angle DBC=\angle BDC=\beta$. Thus $BD$ bisects the angle at $B$. Since $AB=AD$, triangle $ABD$ is isosceles, so $\angle ADB=\angle ABD=\beta=\angle BDC$. Thus $BD$ also bisects the angle at $D$.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Prove that the diagonals meet at right angles.

answer.short:
$AC\perp BD$.

Use the angle bisections from part a and the angle sum of a triangle.
answer.worked:
Let $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $M$, and let $\angle BAC=\alpha$ and $\angle ABD=\beta$. By part a, $\angle BAD=2\alpha$ and $\angle ABC=2\beta$. Since $AD\parallel BC$, $\angle ADB=\angle DBC=\beta$ (alternate angles and part a).

Using the angle sum of triangle $ABD$:
$$\begin{align*}2\alpha+2\beta&=180^\circ\\\alpha+\beta&=90^\circ\end{align*}$$
In triangle $AMB$, $\angle BAM=\alpha$ and $\angle ABM=\beta$. Hence
$$\begin{align*}\angle AMB&=180^\circ-(\alpha+\beta)\\\angle AMB&=180^\circ-90^\circ\\\angle AMB&=90^\circ.\end{align*}$$
Therefore $AC\perp BD$.

children.prompt: Prove that the diagonals are equal.

answer.short:
$AC=BD$.

Both diagonals have square $x^2+y^2$ by Pythagoras’ theorem, where $x$ and $y$ are the rectangle’s side lengths.
answer.worked:
Join $AC$ and $BD$. Let $AB=x$ and $BC=y$. Since opposite sides of a rectangle are equal, $DC=x$.

Using Pythagoras’ theorem in right triangle $ABC$:
$$\begin{align*}AC^2&=AB^2+BC^2\\AC^2&=x^2+y^2.\end{align*}$$
Using Pythagoras’ theorem in right triangle $BCD$:
$$\begin{align*}BD^2&=BC^2+CD^2\\BD^2&=y^2+x^2\\BD^2&=x^2+y^2.\end{align*}$$
Thus $AC^2=BD^2$. Since lengths are positive, $AC=BD$.

entries.description:
First property: the opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal
Theorem: The opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.
Proof: Let ABCD be a parallelogram.
Let ∠A = α.
We need to prove that ∠C = α.
∠D = 180° − α (co-interior angles, AB ∥ DC)
∠C = 180° − ∠D (co-interior angles, AD ∥ BC)
     = 180° − (180° − α)
     = α
Hence, the opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.

entries.description:
Second property: the opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal
Theorem: The opposite sides of a parallelogram are equal.
Proof: Let ABCD be a parallelogram.
We need to prove that AB = BC and AD = BC.
Join the diagonal AC.
In the triangles ABC and CDA:
∠BAC = ∠DCA (alternate angles, AB ∥ DC)
∠BCA = ∠DAC (alternate angles, AD ∥ BC)
AC is common.
So, △ABC ≡ △CDA (AAS)
Hence, AB = CD and BC = AD (matching sides of congruent triangles)

entries.description:
Third property: the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other
Theorem: The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other.
Proof: Let ABCD be a parallelogram.
Let the diagonals AC and BD meet at M.
We need to prove that AM = CM and DM = BM.
In the triangles ABM and CDM:
∠BAM = ∠DCM (alternate angles, AB ∥ DC)
∠ABM = ∠CDM (alternate angles, AB ∥ DC)
AB = CD (opposite sides of parallelogram)
Hence, △ABM ≡ △CDM (AAS)
So AM = CM and DM = BM (matching sides of congruent triangles)
